name: Question 14
problem:
Let $F(x)={x}^{2}$ for $x\in R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)).
$$

Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient ${b}_{2}$ below, where $⟨\,,⟩$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi ,\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{2} & ={{field-1}} \\  & ={{field-2}}\,\cdot \,{{field-3}}\end{aligned}
$$
worked_solution:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi )$ is given by

$$
⟨f(x),g(x)⟩={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)g(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

For a $2\pi $-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi ,\pi ),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by 

$$
f(x)∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),
$$

where ${a}_{0},$ ${a}_{n},$ and ${b}_{n}$ are constants to be determined. 

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }({a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)+{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ ⟨\frac{{a}_{0}}{2},\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }⟨{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & = \\ \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}⟨1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the functions
$1,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x),…$
are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is

$$
{b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩.
$$

Computing the inner product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)]}_{-\pi }^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\pi -(-\pi ))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4\pi ))) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain that

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ & ={b}_{2}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩ \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{⟨f(x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩}{⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x),\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)⟩} \\ {b}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\pi }\cdot {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The usual inner product of functions f and g over x∈[−π,π) is given by ⟨f(x),g(x)⟩=∫−ππf(x)g(x)dx.

For a 2π-periodic function f(x) that is piecewise continuous over x∈[−π,π), the Fourier series of f is given by f(x)∼a02+∑n=1∞(ancos⁡(nx)+bnsin⁡(nx)), where a0, an, and bn are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of f(x) with sin⁡(2x):

⟨f(x),sin⁡(2x)⟩=⟨a02+∑n=1∞(ancos⁡(nx)+bnsin⁡(nx)),sin⁡(2x)⟩=⟨a02,sin⁡(2x)⟩+∑n=1∞⟨ancos⁡(nx),sin⁡(2x)⟩+∑n=1∞⟨bnsin⁡(nx),sin⁡(2x)⟩=a02⟨1,sin⁡(2x)⟩+∑n=1∞an⟨cos⁡(nx),sin⁡(2x)⟩+∑n=1∞bn⟨sin⁡(nx),sin⁡(2x)⟩

Since the functions 1,sin⁡(x),cos⁡(x),sin⁡(2x),cos⁡(2x),… are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is b2⟨sin⁡(2x),sin⁡(2x)⟩.

Computing the inner product, we have ⟨sin⁡(2x),sin⁡(2x)⟩=∫−ππsin2⁡(2x)dx=∫−ππ12−12cos⁡(4x)dx=[12x−18sin⁡(4x)]−ππ=12(π−(−π))−18(sin⁡(4π)−(sin⁡(−4π)))=π.

Finally, we obtain that ⟨f(x),sin⁡(2x)⟩=b2⟨sin⁡(2x),sin⁡(2x)⟩b2=⟨f(x),sin⁡(2x)⟩⟨sin⁡(2x),sin⁡(2x)⟩b2=1π∫−ππf(x)sin⁡(2x)dx=1π⋅∫−ππx2sin⁡(2x)dx.
